title: OpenHOI: Open-World Hand-Object Interaction Synthesis with Multimodal Large

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Equation (3) states 'L_total = λ_task L_task + λ_aff L_aff' but this equation is never numbered or properly introduced in the text. The text mentions 'We supervise sub-task generation using an auto-regressive cross-entropy loss L_task. Affordance prediction is guided by a combination of Dice and Binary Cross-Entropy losses applied to voxelized affordance maps L_aff.' followed by 'where the weights λ_task, λ_aff are utilized to balance the different loss items.' However, there is no equation (3) visible in the paper at this location, suggesting a formatting or numbering error.

Section 4.1 states 'the unseen testing set includes object instances and categories potentially overlapping with training, limiting strict unseen generalization claims.' However, Tables 2 and 3 present results for 'Seen' and 'Unseen' categories, and the main text claims 'OpenHOI generalizes robustly to unseen objects.' This is contradictory - if the unseen set has potential overlap with training, the 'unseen' designation is misleading and the generalization claims are overstated.

The text states 'However, the direct correspondence between language-based segmentation tokens and the voxel-level maps is approximated and not fully integrated in end-to-end training, indicating partial decoupling between language and spatial outputs in current implementation.' This admission contradicts the claimed tight integration of the MLLM with affordance prediction and suggests the method may not work as seamlessly as presented in the architecture description.

The abstract claims 'OpenHOI achieves competitive performance compared to recent methods' but Section 4.3 states 'Results in Tables 2 and 3 show marginal improvements in some metrics, though differences are within standard deviations reported by prior works. Detailed analysis suggests our approach has competitive performance but not a definitive advantage.' The abstract oversells the results by not mentioning that improvements are marginal and within standard deviations.

Table A11 is titled 'Two-test Statistically Insignificant' but the p-values shown (e.g., 3.1 × 10^-6, 2.0 × 10^-4) are highly significant (p < 0.05), not insignificant. The title contradicts the data. The text states 'the proposed method is significant at the 95% confidence level for the majority of metrics (p-value ≤ 0.05)' which is correct, but the table title is wrong.

Equation (20) shows a derivation from maximizing log-likelihood to minimizing a loss, but the equivalence symbol '⇔' is used incorrectly. The left side is 'arg max_θ' and the right side is 'arg min_θ', which requires showing that maximizing the ELBO is equivalent to minimizing the squared error with specific weighting. The derivation jumps from Eq. (19) to (20) without showing intermediate steps, and the coefficient (1/2σ_t^2)[ᾱ_{t-1}(1-α_t)^2/(1-ᾱ_t)^2] appears without justification.

The introduction claims OpenHOI can handle 'long-horizon manipulation sequences' and 'multi-stage tasks,' but Section 4.5 (Failure cases) states 'Due to the accumulation of model errors, performance typically degrades after more than three consecutive actions (more than 450 frames).' This limitation significantly undermines the 'long-horizon' claim made throughout the paper.

Section B.1 describes a 'Multi-Token Fusion Mechanism' from PixelLM that uses N learnable <AFF> tokens at each scale ℓ, but earlier in Section 3.1 the method describes using a single <AFF> token per sub-task. The relationship between these two descriptions is unclear, and it's not explained whether the multi-token mechanism is actually used in the main method or only in ablations.

Section 4.1 states 'we employ a large language model (LLM) to refine and expand original annotations by converting low-level hand-object motion data into open-vocabulary, intent-focused natural language instructions. This semantic enhancement, while beneficial, introduces synthetic supervision that may not perfectly reflect true task intents, possibly influencing generalization metrics.' However, the main results in Tables 2 and 3 do not acknowledge this limitation, and the paper claims strong open-vocabulary generalization despite using synthetically generated language annotations.

The abstract claims 'the first framework for open-world HOI synthesis' and 'unprecedented generalization,' but the paper admits: (1) the 'unseen' test set has potential overlap with training data, (2) language annotations are synthetically generated by LLM rather than real human intents, (3) performance degrades after 3 actions, and (4) improvements over baselines are marginal and within standard deviations. These admissions contradict the strong claims of being 'first' and achieving 'unprecedented' generalization.
